analysis.evidence: וְאֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדֹת תֶּרַח means “and these are the generations of Terah.” The demonstrative points forward to the genealogy that begins by naming Terah’s sons.
analysis.morphology: The conjunction וְ means “and.” אֵלֶּה is a plural demonstrative pronoun of common gender.

analysis.evidence: Carried forward: this word and its source tagging were reviewed identically at 68362:1, 68097:1, 67081:1, 66817:2.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, feminine plural construct, with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: generations, the account of what came from someone

analysis.evidence: The marked תֶּרַח names the man whose family the heading introduces. The following clause repeats his name as the subject of הוֹלִיד and identifies Abram, Nahor, and Haran as his sons.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with no prefix or suffix. The name completes the construct phrase תּוֹלְדֹת תֶּרַח, “the generations of Terah.”
analysis.sense: The father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran.

analysis.evidence: After the heading וְאֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדֹת תֶּרַח, the repeated name begins the clause תֶּרַח הוֹלִיד. The three names introduced by אֶת, אֶת, and וְאֶת identify the sons Terah fathered.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew personal proper noun without a prefix or suffix. This second occurrence of תֶּרַח is the subject of הוֹלִיד.
analysis.sense: The father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran.

analysis.evidence: Terah is the subject of הוֹלִיד. The direct-object marker אֶת introduces each of the three sons he fathered, Abram, Nahor, and Haran.
analysis.morphology: Hiphil perfect, third person masculine singular, agreeing with תֶּרַח.

analysis.evidence: In תֶּרַח הוֹלִיד אֶת אַבְרָם, Terah is the subject of הוֹלִיד ‘fathered’, and אֶת marks the proper name אַבְרָם ‘Abram’ as its definite direct object.
analysis.morphology: Direct-object particle with no prefix or suffix.

draft.change: Link the existing Abram article to אבה through its father element and add Genesis 12:4 as an example.
draft.definition: Abram, son of Terah, later named Abraham. The name means “exalted father.”
draft.evidence: Genesis 12:4 repeats the name אַבְרָם when giving Abram’s age at departure. The name’s אָב element belongs to Haqor’s אבה article.

analysis.evidence: In תֶּרַח הוֹלִיד אֶת אַבְרָם, “Terah fathered Abram,” אַבְרָם names the first of the three sons listed. Haqor links the name to אבה through its אָב element, “father.”
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with no prefix or suffix. The preceding אֶת is a separate direct-object marker.
analysis.sense: Abram, the son of Terah later named Abraham

analysis.evidence: In אֶת אַבְרָם אֶת נָחוֹר וְאֶת הָרָן, the marked אֶת introduces נָחוֹר (Nahor), the second of three coordinated direct objects of הוֹלִיד (“fathered”).
analysis.morphology: Direct-object particle with no prefix or suffix.

draft.change: Add Terah’s son as a second bearer of the name alongside Serug’s son.
draft.definition: Nahor is the personal name borne here by Terah’s son, Abram’s brother and Milcah’s husband.
draft.evidence: Genesis 11:26 lists Abram and Nahor among Terah’s sons. Genesis 11:29 names Milcah as Nahor’s wife.

analysis.evidence: Terah is the subject of הוֹלִיד (“fathered”). The repeated אֶת marks Abram, Nahor, and Haran as its objects, identifying this Nahor as Terah’s son and Abram’s brother.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with no prefix or suffix. The preceding אֶת is a separate direct-object marker.
analysis.sense: Nahor, Abram’s brother and Milcah’s husband

evidence.note: וְאֶת הָרָן closes the list of sons whom Terah fathered.

article.name: הָרָן
article.summary: Genesis 11:26 names Haran among Terah’s sons, alongside Abram and Nahor. The origin of the name is uncertain.

draft.change: Add a personal-name article for הָרָן with the root unassigned.
draft.evidence: Genesis 11:26 names Haran as the third son listed after “he fathered.” The verse gives no etymology for his name.

analysis.evidence: The marked הָרָן is the third son named after “Terah fathered,” following Abram and Nahor. The next clause names the same Haran as Lot’s father. The verse gives no etymology for the name.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew personal name without a prefix or suffix. The preceding וְאֶת is a separate word marking Haran as a direct object of הוֹלִיד.

evidence.note: After listing Haran among Terah’s sons, the genealogy says וְהָרָן הוֹלִיד אֶת לוֹט, “and Haran fathered Lot.”

article.name: הָרָן
article.summary: Genesis 11:27 names Haran alongside Abram and Nahor as a son of Terah. It then identifies him as the father of Lot.

draft.change: Add a personal-name article for הָרָן with the etymology left open.
draft.definition: Haran, the personal name borne here by Terah’s son and Lot’s father.
draft.evidence: Genesis 11:27 identifies Haran through both family relationships. The verse gives no derivation for his name.

analysis.evidence: Terah’s sons are listed as Abram, Nahor and Haran. The marked occurrence repeats the last son’s name as the subject of וְהָרָן הוֹלִיד אֶת לוֹט, “and Haran fathered Lot.”
analysis.morphology: The conjunction וְ joins the clauses. The personal name הָרָן is the subject of הוֹלִיד, “fathered.”
analysis.sense: Haran, son of Terah and father of Lot

analysis.evidence: In וְהָרָן הוֹלִיד אֶת לוֹט, Haran is the subject and אֶת marks Lot as the direct object. The clause identifies Haran as Lot’s father.
analysis.morphology: Hiphil perfect, third person masculine singular, agreeing with Haran.

analysis.evidence: In וְהָרָן הוֹלִיד אֶת לוֹט, “and Haran fathered Lot,” אֶת marks the personal name לוֹט as the definite direct object of הוֹלִיד.
analysis.morphology: Direct-object particle with no prefix or suffix.

evidence.note: Terah fathered Abram, Nahor and Haran, and Haran fathered Lot.

article.name: לוֹט
article.summary: Terah’s genealogy names Lot as Haran’s son and Abram’s nephew. The passage gives no explanation of the name.

draft.change: Add a personal-name article for לוֹט with its etymology unassigned.
draft.evidence: Genesis 11:27 names Lot as the son whom Haran fathered.

analysis.evidence: The clause וְהָרָן הוֹלִיד אֶת לוֹט means “and Haran fathered Lot.” It repeats the construction used earlier in the verse to name Terah’s sons. The genealogy identifies Lot but gives no derivation for his name.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew personal proper noun with no prefix or suffix. The separate particle אֶת marks לוֹט as the direct object of הוֹלִיד.
analysis.sense: The personal name of Haran’s son.
